prize_parts.citation: For the invention of the optical lattice clock based on magic-wavelength trapping and its realisation at the 10^-18 level of accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: After reading the full first round I keep B042 as a single-achievement prize to Katori and Ye, and my confidence is slightly higher than before because the objections raised are about framing and not about the physics. The core is a physical insight: at the magic wavelength the lattice shifts the two clock levels equally, so thousands of atoms can be held tightly and interrogated at once without Doppler, recoil or first-order light-shift errors. Katori proposed it and his group made the first strontium demonstration. The record-setting realisation, with the stability and the control of blackbody, lattice and collisional shifts that took the clocks to the 1e-18 level, came from Ye's group, and other laboratories (SYRTE, PTB, RIKEN and Tokyo, NIST) have reproduced and compared that performance. That reproducibility is what I value most. The consequences are results about nature: gravitational redshift resolved over millimetres, tighter limits on drifting constants, and searches for ultralight dark matter. I can check the systematic budgets directly, and I find them sound. As I read the chair's questions, a citation worded around the lattice clock and not the comb or the redefinition of the second answers the overlap concern with 2005 and 2012.
statement.case_against: The honest weakness remains the discovery-versus-instrument reading. Mehlig and Olsson weigh the clock nearer to a decisive performance advance than to a new regime of physics, and I cannot dismiss that, since the frequency comb (2005) and ion control (2012) sit directly beside it. The attribution is also not perfectly tidy: Takamoto, Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom and the PTB and SYRTE groups made decisive demonstrations, and a two-name prize will look incomplete to some in the community. If the committee judges the redefinition of the second to be the real milestone, it may prefer to wait. Finally, I am an atomic theorist and may overvalue precision, so I have tried to test my case against colleagues who do not share that taste. I do not think these points defeat the case, but they are real.

responses.point: Pearce asked whether anyone beyond Katori and Ye has a priority claim on the earliest lattice-clock demonstrations, and said he would like to know before the vote.
responses.response: I went through the record as I remember it, and I would flag that this should be checked against the papers. The magic-wavelength proposal is Katori's, and the first strontium lattice spectroscopy came from his group, in which Takamoto was a student and first author. The JILA strontium lattice clock followed within a short time, and SYRTE worked in parallel on strontium and mercury. Those later groups confirmed and refined the idea; they did not originate it. The decisive step for the 1e-18 regime was Ye's, in the sense of cavity-stabilised interrogation and systematic control, which is what the other laboratories are compared against. I therefore do not see a competing originator who would change the pair. Lemonde and the PTB group are important confirming contributors, and the citation can acknowledge the concept and its realisation without naming them. Your concern about Ye twice in a short span with the thorium clock is a strategic question I would not let drive today's choice.

responses.point: Johansson asked whether I see the lattice clocks (B042) and the Hubbard-model quantum simulators (B050) as complementary or as competing for the same slot, and noted that he defers to me on credit between Ye and the other groups.
responses.response: I see them as different in content though they share the AMO label. B050 is a prize for a platform for emulating many-body Hamiltonians, and as Kroll and Eriksson both noted, its credit is contested between the experimentalists and Zoller, and B038 draws on the same Zoller contribution, so I would not choose it this year. The clock is a measurement that shows nature at a precision nobody had before. I would not treat the AMO cluster as a single group that can have only one prize. On credit between Ye and the others, the discriminating question is who made the 1e-18 performance real. The answer is Ye's group, and I would keep Katori as the originator. I would still prefer to say in the citation what the pair did and avoid listing other groups.

responses.point: Mehlig reads the lattice clock as a decisive performance advance and not as a new regime of physics, since combs (2005) and ion clocks (2012) are already recognised, whereas moire flat bands are a new mechanism. Mehlig keeps B042 as the first alternative and would not strongly object to it.
responses.response: I take that seriously and it is the strongest argument against my position, so I would like to answer on the physics. What is new is not the accuracy as such. The magic wavelength turns a trapped many-atom ensemble into a quantum-limited oscillator, with stability that single-ion clocks cannot reach, which allows comparison of clock rates across a millimetre in a gravitational field. That is a regime in which one measures a relativistic effect locally, and it is not something the 2005 or 2012 prizes made available. I agree that twisted bilayer graphene is new physics, but I would still not want to reward it while the pairing mechanism is unsettled. I am glad you would not object strongly to B042, and we agree that the citation should state what the clock is for and nothing more.

responses.point: Olsson asks what Ye's record-setting clocks add that is original and not only superior to Katori's concept, and calls B042 the cleaner and more mature alternative to B019.
responses.response: I think the distinction between original and superior is fair, and I would answer it this way. Katori's idea defines what a lattice clock is. Ye's group demonstrated that its limits are not those expected of a many-atom system, by controlling collisions with a degenerate, spin-polarised gas and by reducing the blackbody uncertainty to the level where 1e-18 becomes a measurement and not a claim. That work changed what was thought possible, and it made the clock a tool for physics, not only a better standard. It is the kind of contribution that I think the will's wording on important improvements can reasonably cover. I agree that B042 is the more mature case compared with B019, and I would not like to see the two put against each other on novelty alone, since they are different kinds of result.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B019 but would not choose it over B042 if the committee concludes that the moire pairing physics is too unsettled, and agrees that B050 and B038 should not be split.
responses.response: Thank you, this is helpful, and we agree on the structure: the two leading cases are B042 and B019, and each of us can accept the other. My own view is that the flat-band prediction and the observed correlated insulators and superconductivity are secure enough to be a discovery, and that the pairing mechanism is not needed for a narrow citation, as you say. What makes me prefer B042 this year is the unresolved credit among Yuan Cao, Dean, Young, Efetov and the earlier Lopes dos Santos theory, which I am not able to judge as well as you and Mehlig can. If the committee decides that B019 can be done with the three names and the citation as proposed, I can support it, and I have kept it as my first alternative.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as a discovery or invention that satisfies the will, given the 2005 and 2012 prizes. This is a question of judgement that I cannot settle by further analysis.

My recollection of the order and timing of the early lattice-clock demonstrations at RIKEN, JILA, SYRTE and PTB is from memory and is not exact. It should be checked against the record before the vote.
How much weight the committee gives to waiting for the redefinition of the second, and whether naming only two people understates the contribution of the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups.
Whether the B019 credit questions (Cao and the earlier twist-angle theory) can be resolved by citation wording, which I cannot judge as well as my condensed-matter colleagues.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with Katori or Ye: I have no collaboration, supervisory link or shared institution with either. I disclose again for transparency that I am a theoretical atomic physicist in an adjacent AMO area, a long-time collaborator of 2023 laureate Anne L'Huillier, and that I work with Lund and ETH attosecond groups, none of whom are on this shortlist. I also note my possible taste for precision physics, which the other members have been able to weigh in their own judgement.
